title: Scheme tests for proper and locally quasi-finite representable stack morphisms
statement:
Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] and let $f:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be a morphism of Deligne--Mumford stacks over $S$, with stacks, scheme atlases and 2-fibre products as in [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. Assume that $f$ is representable by schemes: for every scheme $T$ and morphism $T\to\mathcal B$, the 2-fibre product $A_T=\mathcal A\times_{\mathcal B}T$ is represented by a scheme. Write $f_T:A_T\to T$ for its projection. Then $f$ is proper if and only if $f_T$ is proper for every scheme $T\to\mathcal B$. Independently, $f$ is locally quasi-finite if and only if $f_T$ is locally quasi-finite for every scheme $T\to\mathcal B$.

Here scheme properness and local quasi-finiteness are [def-weil-proper-morphism, pqf-def-quasifinite], including local finite type in the latter notion. For stacks, locally of finite type is tested on smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] scheme charts using [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and finite type additionally requires quasi-compactness. Proper means finite type, universally closed, and having proper relative diagonal. Universally closed means that every base change induces a closed map of underlying point spaces. Locally quasi-finite means locally of finite type, with locally quasi-finite relative diagonal and discrete underlying point space of every field fibre. The point space consists of field-valued objects up to isomorphism and common field extension, with topology detected by an atlas. Algebraic spaces use [def-trf-algebraic-space]; properties of representable diagonals are tested on scheme charts. No finiteness assumption on $f$ is made.

source.place: Tag 04YS (lemma-representable-separated-diagonal-closed); Tag 06UA (lemma-representable-by-spaces-quasi-finite), with Tag 06PU (definition-locally-quasi-finite); discussion immediately after Tag 0CL5 (definition-proper), explicitly identifying properness for representable morphisms with scheme/algebraic-space tests. Representable-by-schemes specialization of these compatibility results; etale-stack/scheme-atlas convention.

proof.text: Regard every scheme as its representable algebraic space by [def-trf-scheme-algebraic-space]. Scheme representability of $f$ therefore supplies the weaker representability hypothesis of the three comparison nodes. First, [lem-sfb-stack-finite-type-calculus] identifies finite type of $f$ with finite type of every $f_T$, including quasi-compactness and agreement with the ordinary algebraic-space notion. Second, apply [lem-sfb-representable-stack-diagonal-criterion] to the relative diagonal $\Delta_f:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\times_{\mathcal B}\mathcal A$: it is proper after every scheme base change if and only if all the maps $f_T$ are separated. Since $A_T$ and $T$ are schemes, their diagonals are the scheme diagonals. Third, [lem-sfb-representable-stack-universally-closed-test] equates intrinsic universal closedness of $f$ with universal closedness of all $f_T$ as algebraic-space maps. Its final compatibility clause gives the ordinary notion for these scheme maps. These are three independent equivalences; none assumes properness or local quasi-finiteness of $f$.

source.place: Finite-type compatibility in section-finite-type (Tag 06FM); Tag 04YS, lemma-representable-separated-diagonal-closed; Tag 0512, lemma-characterize-representable-universally-closed; Tag 0CL3, lemma-universally-closed-local

proof.text: Suppose first that $f$ is intrinsically proper. Its finite type, proper relative diagonal and universal closedness give, by the three equivalences of step 1, finite type, separatedness and universal closedness of each $f_T$. Thus every $f_T$ is proper by [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Conversely suppose every $f_T$ is proper. That definition gives all three scheme properties for each $T$. Applying the reverse directions of the three equivalences in step 1 separately gives finite type of $f$, properness of its relative diagonal on all scheme tests, and intrinsic universal closedness of $f$. Thus $f$ is finite type, has proper relative diagonal, and is universally closed, which is intrinsic properness. In particular no single scheme test is assumed to imply properness; the converse uses the whole quantified family, and quasi-compactness remains part of finite type.

source.place: Tag 0CL5, definition-proper and its following compatibility discussion; scheme definition: morphisms.tex Tag 01W1, definition-proper

proof.text: Assume now, independently, that $f$ is locally quasi-finite. Fix any scheme $T\to\mathcal B$. By hypothesis $A_T$ is a scheme. Its identity is an etale scheme chart (indeed a surjective chart), using its representable algebraic-space structure [def-trf-scheme-algebraic-space]. Apply implication (a) to (b) of [lem-sfb-dm-lqf-atlas-test] with $V=T$ and $U=A_T$ and this identity chart. The composite $U\to V$ is exactly $f_T$, so $f_T$ is locally quasi-finite in the scheme sense [pqf-def-quasifinite], which includes local finite type. The chosen map $T\to\mathcal B$ need not itself be etale or surjective.

source.place: Tag 06UF, lemma-characterize-locally-quasi-finite, implication (1) to (2), specialized to DM etale charts; Tag 06PU, definition-locally-quasi-finite

proof.text: Conversely, suppose every scheme test $f_T$ is locally quasi-finite. The DM hypothesis on $\mathcal B$ supplies a surjective etale scheme atlas $V\to\mathcal B$ by [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. Apply the hypothesis to this particular map: representability makes $A_V$ a scheme and its projection $f_V:A_V\to V$ is locally quasi-finite. By [def-trf-scheme-algebraic-space] the identity of this scheme is a surjective etale scheme atlas of $\mathcal A\times_{\mathcal B}V$. Thus $U=A_V$ and this identity, together with the chosen target atlas, satisfy condition (c) of [lem-sfb-dm-lqf-atlas-test]. The composite $U\to V$ is exactly $f_V$. Implication (c) to (a) of that criterion gives intrinsic local quasi-finiteness of $f$. Neither direction of this clause uses quasi-compactness, properness or global finite type.
